nodes.title: A Note to the Reader
nodes.heading: chapter
text: This is a book about quantum mechanics, but it begins with a more ordinary problem: a record can be accurate and still leave out exactly what matters next.

A scoreboard tells us who won, but not how the game unfolded. A map of airline traffic tells us where people arrived, but not which conversations occurred in transit. A probability tells us how often an outcome appears, but not necessarily how the process that produced it can be joined to another process. The missing information may remain harmless until we ask the system to continue. Then the omission returns as a surprise.

The technical monograph behind this book studies that surprise using stochastic, bistochastic, orthostochastic, and unistochastic matrices. Those terms will appear here, but none is required at the door. The essential ideas are simpler: probabilities are projections of richer processes; projections may fail to preserve composition; locally acceptable descriptions may fail to fit together globally; and the mathematics of quantum theory can be approached as a disciplined response to those failures.

This is not a claim that quantum mechanics follows from probability alone. It does not. The reconstruction begins with a consequential choice about which probabilistic transformations count as admissible. Later it adds further commitments about systems, states, measurements, and time. One purpose of this companion is to keep those costs visible. The result is not inevitability, but intelligibility: a view of quantum formalism as an architecture built to preserve coherence across transformations that probability alone cannot compose.

Readers who want proofs should consult the technical monograph. Readers who want to know what the proofs mean, what they do not mean, and why the pattern matters beyond quantum foundations are in the right place.

nodes.title: The Honest Shadow
nodes.heading: chapter
text: A probability can be perfectly honest. It can be measured carefully, reported exactly, and confirmed a thousand times. Yet honesty is not completeness. The central mistake examined in this book is the assumption that because a probability faithfully records an outcome, it must also faithfully record the process that connects one outcome-producing situation to another.

Imagine a machine with several labelled lamps. Feed it the same input many times and it illuminates one lamp on each trial. After enough trials we can construct a table: input one produces lamp A half the time and lamp B half the time; input two produces some other distribution. This table is operationally meaningful. It predicts frequencies. It can be checked without knowing anything about the inside of the machine.

Now place two such machines in sequence. It is tempting to predict the final lamps by multiplying their probability tables. Sometimes that works. It works when each stage merely passes classical alternatives forward, as though a concealed but definite route were chosen at the first stage and inherited by the second. But there are other processes for which the first table is not a sufficient description of what the second machine receives. Two internal contributions that led to the same visible probability can later reinforce or cancel each other. The first table was not false. It was a shadow whose missing depth mattered only when the process continued.

This is the conceptual location of quantum interference. Interference is often introduced as an alien property of microscopic objects, accompanied by waves that are particles and particles that are waves. That imagery can be useful, but it can also obscure the logical issue. The more basic fact is that the probability projection forgets relational information. When transformations are composed, the forgotten information affects the next probability distribution.

The word projection matters. A projection is not necessarily an error or an approximation. A photograph projects a three-dimensional scene onto two dimensions while remaining an exact photograph. Trouble begins only when we ask the photograph to answer a question whose answer depends on depth. Likewise, a transition-probability matrix may answer every question about a single observed transition while failing to determine the result of two transitions in sequence.

The book's guiding question is therefore not, “Why is nature probabilistic?” It is narrower and, in some ways, stranger: What additional structure must survive behind probabilities if transformations are to compose coherently? That question turns quantum mechanics from a catalogue of oddities into a problem of information preservation.
An observable record can be sufficient for prediction at one stage and insufficient for continuation. Sufficiency is indexed to the operation we intend to perform next.

This shift also changes what counts as an explanation. A probability table is a witness: it records that some transformation occurred and summarizes its visible consequences. A mechanism is something stronger: it supports counterfactual continuation, tells us how transformations combine, and distinguishes processes that cast the same probabilistic shadow. Confusing the witness with the mechanism makes quantum interference look like probability behaving irrationally. Separating them reveals something more precise. Probability behaves exactly as promised; we asked it to retain information it was never designed to carry.

Statisticians have a name for exactly this kind of task-relative sufficiency, and it predates quantum mechanics by decades. A sufficient statistic is a summary of data that loses nothing relevant to one particular question, typically the value of some parameter, while discarding everything else about the raw data. The average of a set of measurements can be a sufficient statistic for the true underlying value being measured, even though it throws away every individual reading. Nobody considers this throwing-away a scandal, because the statistic was never asked to answer any other question. The trouble in quantum mechanics is structurally the same and differs only in scale: a probability table is sufficient for one question, namely what happens if this transformation is used once and never composed with anything else, and insufficient for a different, entirely reasonable question, namely what happens if it is composed. Sufficiency was never a property of the data alone. It was always a property of the data relative to a stated use, and probability tables are no exception.

nodes.title: A World Made of Columns
nodes.heading: chapter
text: The simplest probability space is a list of alternatives whose weights add to one. If there are three possible outcomes, the state of our uncertainty might be written as seventy percent, twenty percent, and ten percent. Geometrically, every such list occupies a point inside a triangle called a probability simplex. Nothing mystical is hidden here. The simplex is simply the space of all legal assignments of weight to mutually exclusive alternatives.

A stochastic matrix moves one probability distribution to another. Each column says what happens to one initial alternative. The entries are nonnegative, and the relevant sums equal one. Classical probability theory becomes, in part, a study of these legal movements through the simplex.

A smaller and more orderly class consists of bistochastic matrices. In a bistochastic matrix, both columns and rows sum to one. Such a transformation preserves the uniform distribution. It can mix distinctions but cannot create a preference for one label merely from uniform ignorance. Every bistochastic matrix is a weighted mixture of permutations: beneath the mixing lies a lottery over rearrangements.

That fact is sometimes read too quickly. It does not say that every individual system secretly undergoes one definite permutation. It says that the matrix lies in the convex hull of permutation matrices. The geometry permits a classical mixture representation. Whether that representation names a physical mechanism is a separate question.

Bistochastic transformations also organize probability distributions by majorization. A sharply concentrated distribution can be mixed into a flatter one, but a bistochastic map cannot turn a flatter distribution into a sharper one without some additional resource. Entropy therefore does not decrease under this kind of mixing. This gives the first important constraint in the reconstruction: admissible probability changes are not arbitrary. They preserve normalization, positivity, and a particular direction of informational mixing.

Yet bistochasticity is still too broad to reproduce quantum structure. Quantum transition matrices belong to a more restricted class. They arise by taking a unitary matrix, a reversible transformation of amplitudes, and replacing every entry by its squared magnitude. Such matrices are called unistochastic.

The definition is compact, but philosophically expensive. It says that a probability table counts as admissible when it can be lifted to a unitary amplitude transformation. This does not derive the unitary world from neutral probability. It chooses a probability class whose membership is certified by the existence of unitary structure. Much of the subsequent reconstruction then explores the consequences of taking this class seriously.

That is not a defect if it is stated plainly. Scientific explanations often begin by identifying a constrained family and asking what follows from membership in it. The danger comes from forgetting that the constraint was selected. “Unistochastic” is not merely a technical adjective attached after the fact. It is the hinge of the project: probability is admitted only when a coherent reversible lift exists above it.

The simplest two-outcome case conceals how strong this choice is. Every two-by-two bistochastic matrix has both a real orthogonal lift and a complex unitary lift. At this size, the visible table cannot distinguish the scalar field. With three outcomes the coincidence breaks. The uniform three-by-three matrix has a complex lift supplied by the discrete Fourier transform, but it has no real orthogonal lift. The obstruction is elementary: a real lift would require a three-by-three array of plus and minus signs whose distinct rows were mutually orthogonal, and no such array exists.

Already we meet two kinds of absence. Sometimes a probability table admits many hidden lifts and therefore underdetermines the mechanism. Sometimes it admits a complex lift but no lift of the more restrictive real kind. The first absence is lost information. The second is failed admissibility. They will matter differently once systems are joined.

There is a well-known picture, familiar to anyone who has seen a single quantum bit drawn as a small sphere, that makes the two-outcome coincidence easier to hold in mind. The full space of states available to one quantum bit is often drawn as a solid ball: every point inside or on its surface is a legitimate state, and the boundary surface itself is the special case of maximal information, a pure state. A bare two-outcome probability table, the kind discussed in this chapter, corresponds to knowing only how far a point sits from the ball's center along a single axis, nothing about the other two directions. At that resolution, real and complex descriptions of the same physical bit genuinely cannot be told apart, because the missing directions are exactly what a real orthogonal lift and a complex unitary lift would disagree about, and neither is visible in a single transition table between two outcomes. The disagreement becomes visible only once more than two outcomes, or more than one context, enters the picture, which is exactly the content of the next two chapters.

nodes.title: The Lift Above the Record
nodes.heading: chapter
text: A lift is a richer object that projects down to the data we observe. Cartographers use lifts implicitly when several flat maps are understood as views of one curved surface. Computer graphics reconstructs three-dimensional scenes from two-dimensional images. In quantum theory, amplitudes play the role of the richer coordinates, while observed probabilities arise from their squared magnitudes.

Why use amplitudes at all? One answer is historical: the formalism works. Another invokes waves: amplitudes interfere as waves do. The reconstruction pursued here offers a structural answer. Amplitudes carry precisely the kind of relational information that probability projection erases but composition requires.

Consider two routes leading from an initial alternative to a final outcome. At the probability level, we might add the probability of route one to the probability of route two. At the amplitude level, we first add the contributions and then square the magnitude. Squaring a sum produces not only the separate squared terms but cross terms. These terms register the relation between the contributions. Depending on that relation, the same two magnitudes can reinforce one another or cancel.

Calling the relation “phase” is useful but can make it sound like a decorative dial attached to a probability. Phase is better understood here as compositional memory. It records distinctions among processes that currently yield the same visible weights but will behave differently when combined with later transformations.

This makes a lift neither a hidden classical trajectory nor an occult substance. It is a bookkeeping structure adequate to continuation. The quantum state need not be imagined as a tiny material wave sloshing through an inaccessible space. At minimum, it is the kind of representation in which transformations close under composition without discarding distinctions that future operations can reveal.

There is an important caution. Many lifts can share the same projection. If every complex entry is replaced by its magnitude squared, signs and phases disappear. Observed probabilities therefore do not usually identify a unique amplitude transformation. The lift solves the problem of closure only after a compatible lift has been chosen. Probability data alone may not tell us which choice is correct.

This gives rise to the next question. A single edge between two experimental contexts may possess an admissible lift. But if we assemble many such edges, can their lifts all belong to one common world? Local existence does not guarantee global compatibility. The issue is no longer whether each photograph could depict some three-dimensional scene. It is whether all the photographs could depict the same scene.

nodes.title: Why Probabilities Do Not Compose
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Suppose a transformation carries alternatives from context A to context B, and another carries them from B to C. At the amplitude level the two transformations multiply. Their product is again a valid transformation. Reversibility and normalization are preserved. The formalism is closed under continuation.

Project each transformation separately into a probability table, however, and multiply those tables. In general the result differs from projecting the already-composed amplitude transformation. The order of operations matters: compose and then forget is not the same as forget and then compose.

This noncommutation is the book's central engine. It is not a peculiarity confined to complex numbers. Real orthogonal amplitudes also produce cross terms, and their squared entries also fail to compose as ordinary stochastic matrices. Interference therefore does not by itself prove that amplitudes must be complex. What it proves is that probability-level description is not compositionally complete.

A vivid example uses two transformations that each look maximally random when viewed alone. Every input has equal probability of producing either output. Classical multiplication predicts that two such stages remain maximally random. Yet suitable amplitude lifts can compose to the identity: after two apparently randomizing operations, the original alternative returns with certainty. The uncertainty was a feature of the projected description, not an irreversible destruction of structure.

This resembles encrypting a message with a reversible cipher and then describing only the frequency of letters. The frequency table may look thoroughly mixed, but a second transformation equipped with the relevant relational structure can recover the original. Nothing supernatural occurred. The summary statistics ceased to be sufficient.

The implication reaches beyond textbook interference experiments. Whenever we compress a process into observables and later attempt to compose those observables, we should ask whether the compression is a homomorphism: does it preserve the operation we care about? If not, apparent novelty at the composed level may be the return of discarded structure.

This principle applies to scientific models, institutional records, and machine-learning representations. Averaging several measurements can preserve their mean while destroying covariance needed for a later prediction. Aggregating votes by district can preserve winners while destroying coalition structure needed to forecast a new election. Summarizing a conversation can preserve propositions while destroying the sequence that determines how a later remark will be understood. In each case the summary may be locally faithful and compositionally unfaithful.

Quantum mechanics supplies an unusually exact instance. The lost terms can be written, manipulated, and tested. But the broader lesson is methodological: a representation should be judged not only by what it reports now, but by which future operations it allows us to perform without contradiction.

nodes.title: Interference as Returning Memory
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Interference is often described as if alternatives literally knew about one another. A photon passing through one slit somehow responds to the presence of another slit; a particle takes all paths; observation reaches backward and changes what occurred. These stories attempt to translate a formal pattern into ordinary objects, sometimes at the cost of making the pattern less clear.

The projection view begins elsewhere. Before measurement, the alternatives are represented within a structure that retains their relative orientation. Measurement produces a probability record that omits part of that orientation. If the alternatives are recombined before the final record is made, the retained relations affect the result. Interference is not the probability table changing its mind. It is evidence that the table was never the whole state of the process.

The word memory must be used carefully. Phase does not necessarily store a narrative of past events. It is memory in a minimal operational sense: two systems with the same present probability distribution can react differently to the same subsequent transformation. Their future dispositions depend on information not present in the probability vector. Something about the path into the present remains available to continuation.

This is a useful criterion for state. A complete state description should screen off the relevant past: once the state is specified, no additional history should improve predictions of future behavior. A bare quantum probability distribution fails this test. The amplitude state can pass it for the transformations included in the theory. The state vector is therefore not merely a convenient encoding of current chances; it repairs a failure of probabilistic Markov sufficiency.

The result also clarifies collapse. A measurement update is not simply the revelation of a probability that was already sitting in the system. It changes which compositional distinctions remain available. Some phase relations are rendered inaccessible relative to the subsequent measurement arrangement. From this perspective, collapse marks a change in the admissible continuation structure, whether that change is treated as physical, informational, relational, or effective.

Nothing in this argument chooses among all interpretations of quantum mechanics. It does not decide whether the wavefunction is ontic, epistemic, relational, many-branched, or agent-relative. It establishes a pressure any interpretation must answer: the theory needs more than a current list of outcome probabilities because future experiments are sensitive to relations that list omits.

Interpretations differ over what bears those relations and what measurement does to them. The compositional diagnosis comes first. It tells us why some additional structure is necessary before telling us what the structure ultimately is.

nodes.title: The Triangle That Refuses to Close
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Pairwise compatibility is reassuring. If every pair of descriptions fits, we are tempted to assume the whole collection fits. This inference fails in many domains. Three maps can agree on overlapping streets yet assign incompatible orientations around a loop. Three witnesses can tell mutually consistent pairwise stories that cannot all occupy a single timeline. Three local coordinate charts can each be well formed while failing to glue into one global object.

Measurement contexts exhibit the same distinction. Represent each context as a vertex of a graph and each observed transition as an edge. An edge is individually admissible when some lift realizes its probability table. A graph is globally realizable when a single assignment of frames to all vertices realizes every edge at once.

On a tree, a connected graph with no loops, local admissibility is enough. Choose a starting frame and move outward. Each edge introduces a new vertex, and there is only one route to it. No alternative route can return with a conflicting demand.

The first genuine test appears when an edge closes a cycle. Now a frame reached along one path must agree with the frame implied by another. At the amplitude level, transformations around a closed loop must compose to the identity, up to the appropriate gauge freedoms. After projection to probabilities, the information needed to verify that equality directly has been lost.

In two real dimensions, three contexts form the smallest cycle. Each pair can have a perfectly valid real transition table, while the three tables together admit no common real assignment. A particularly sharp example asks for three pairwise mutually unbiased real bases. Any two such bases exist. All three do not. Complex two-dimensional space supplies the missing freedom and permits the familiar triple associated with the three Pauli measurements.

This triangle is important because it separates two claims that are easily confused. There is no problem with any edge considered alone. The obstruction belongs to their attempted gluing. Complex structure is not introduced merely to decorate each local transition. It enlarges the space of globally compatible arrangements.

The pattern can be phrased as an inheritance failure. Admissibility does not automatically pass from parts to wholes. Local witnesses do not inherit global consistency. A cycle asks a question no individual edge can answer: after moving through a sequence of perspectives, have we returned to the same frame?

That question has geometric echoes in holonomy, gauge theory, and curvature. Carrying an orientation around a loop may return it altered, revealing structure invisible along any isolated segment. The monograph's context graphs are elementary compared with those theories, but they share the same conceptual grammar. Global information can live in the failure of local comparisons to close.

Mutually unbiased bases are not merely foundational curiosities. They are resources in quantum state tomography and quantum cryptography, because information encoded sharply in one basis appears maximally uncertain when interrogated in another. The best-known cryptographic protocol, BB84, uses two such bases, a structure already available over the reals in two dimensions, since any two mutually unbiased bases can be found without needing a third. A later variant, the six-state protocol, uses the full triple of Pauli bases at once, which brings it much closer to the complex three-context geometry this chapter has been discussing. The real MUB obstruction does not, by itself, prove the security of either protocol. What it identifies is a structural resource available to the complex two-level theory, a genuine triple of mutually unbiased bases, that no globally real two-dimensional description can reproduce, whatever protocol is eventually built on top of it.

nodes.title: Trees, Cycles, and the Cost of Agreement
nodes.heading: chapter
text: A tree is easy not because its edges are simple, but because it never demands reconciliation. Every new edge extends the existing assignment into untouched territory. A cycle is difficult because it creates a second account of something already assigned.

This makes cycle rank a measure of independent agreement conditions. Begin with a spanning tree connecting all contexts. Every remaining edge closes one fundamental cycle. Each such edge asks whether the frame already implied by the tree predicts the observed transition. If the answer is no, no global realization exists for that choice of lifts.

The test is shared, not edgewise. When several cycles overlap, one cannot choose phases or signs independently to satisfy each loop. The same tree lifts must satisfy all non-tree edges simultaneously. Global consistency is a coordination problem among constraints that reuse common structure.

Under a natural model in two real dimensions, the effect is severe. Give each edge an independently chosen continuous transition angle. As soon as the graph contains a cycle, the probability of exact global real realizability is zero. The final edge of a loop must land on one of finitely many values determined by the earlier edges. A continuously drawn number hits that finite target set with probability zero.

This does not mean that physical experiments almost surely contradict real quantum theory. Physical data are not generated by choosing every pairwise transition independently. If contexts arise from an underlying set of real frames, their edges are correlated by construction and every cycle closes. The measure-zero result instead exposes how much coordination a global model imposes. Realizability occupies a thin surface inside the much larger space of independently specifiable local data.

The distinction between generated data and arbitrary data is crucial. A model may fit every dataset produced within itself while occupying a very special region of the logically possible observations. Calling that region “fine-tuned” may or may not be justified; what is justified is recognizing its codimension. Global coherence is purchased by correlations among local records.

This also changes how one should think about experimental tests. A single transition can distinguish real from complex lifts in dimensions three and above, but not in dimension two. There, one needs a cycle: several contexts whose joint relations create an obstruction. The minimal test depends on a low-dimensional coincidence. Once dimension increases, the cheapest witness can collapse back to a single edge.

At two dimensions specifically, the trees-versus-cycles distinction turns out to be a complete classification, not merely a useful rule of thumb, though the precise statement needs care. It is not that every labelling of a cyclic graph fails to be realized: correlated labellings generated from an underlying family of real frames realize perfectly well, since they were built to be consistent from the start. Rather, every individually admissible edge labelling is guaranteed to be globally real-realizable if and only if the graph is a forest. Once a graph contains a cycle, some admissible labellings fail to glue, and, as the earlier discussion of independently drawn edge angles showed, the labellings that do glue occupy only a measure-zero sliver of the labellings that could have been drawn. Cycles are therefore not graphs on which realization never occurs. They are exactly the graphs on which edgewise admissibility, by itself, stops being enough to guarantee it.

The mechanism that proves this is a stretching trick, and it is short enough to see directly. Take the mutually unbiased triangle on contexts Z, X, Y, with all three canonical angles set to π/4, the configuration already shown to admit no real realization. Now insert a new context W directly along the edge between Z and Y, and split that one edge into two: an edge from Z to W carrying angle zero, meaning W is simply aligned with Z and nothing changes there, and an edge from W to Y carrying the original angle of π/4 that used to sit on the edge from Z to Y directly. Nothing about the observed data has been altered; the composite transition from Z through W to Y still amounts to exactly the same π/4 it always did, since composing an identity step with the original step changes nothing.

The result is a four-cycle, Z to X to Y to W back to Z, carrying angles π/4, π/4, π/4, and zero. Suppose this four-cycle had a real realization after all. Restricting that same frame assignment to just Z, X, and Y would then realize the original triangle too, because the zero-angle edge forces W's frame to coincide exactly with Z's, so nothing about a hypothetical solution to the larger cycle could have avoided also solving the smaller one. Since the triangle has no real solution, neither does the stretched square. The identical trick, applied again to any edge of the square, produces a failing pentagon, and repeating it produces a failing cycle of every length beyond that.

So every cycle length inherits a genuinely unrealizable labelling from the original triangle, by nothing more than inserting harmless identity steps along one edge at a time. And once a cycle anywhere inside a larger graph carries such a labelling, the whole graph inherits the failure too: any global frame assignment realizing every edge of the full graph would, in particular, have to realize every edge of that one troublesome cycle sitting inside it, which has already been shown to be impossible. What happens on the rest of the graph, however large or however tamely behaved, cannot rescue a cycle that was built to fail on its own.

Put the two directions together and the classification is exact. Trees never close a loop, so an admissible labelling on a tree always glues, with no exceptions, by the same argument used throughout this chapter. Any graph containing a cycle can be given a labelling, built by the stretching trick above, that individually passes every single edge test yet fails to glue as a whole. A two-dimensional context graph guarantees realizability for every admissible labelling exactly when it has no cycle to exploit in the first place, that is, exactly when it is a forest. This does not make cyclic graphs uniformly dangerous. It makes them exactly, and only, the graphs where danger is possible at all.

The moral is not that cycles are universally quantum. It is that cycles convert continuation into consistency. Whenever local transformations are quotients of richer structure, loops are natural detectors of what the quotient forgot.

nodes.title: Interlude: The Arithmetic So Far
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Everything claimed so far in this book can be checked directly, with nothing more than ordinary arithmetic. This interlude collects three such calculations, one for each of the last three chapters. None of it is required to follow the rest of the book, and a reader satisfied with the prose argument can turn straight to the next part, on joining separate systems together, without losing the thread. But for a reader who wants to see, in plain numbers, that these claims are not merely plausible but exact, the arithmetic is short enough to write out in full.

nodes.title: The Vanishing Uncertainty
nodes.heading: section
text: Take two very small transformations, each a two-by-two matrix built entirely from entries of size one over the square root of two, so that every single entry, squared, gives a fifty-fifty probability:
[equation]
Multiply them together at the amplitude level, in the order U_2U_1, and every cross term collapses cleanly:
[equation]
Squaring the magnitude of this product gives the identity probability table exactly: input one always produces output one, input two always produces output two, with no uncertainty left at all.

Now compare this with what happens if the two probability tables are multiplied directly, ignoring the amplitudes. Squaring U_1 and U_2 entrywise gives the same fully mixed table for both, 121&1 1&1, and this matrix is idempotent: multiplying it by itself returns the identical fully mixed matrix, never the identity. Two machines that look, on paper, like they each randomize their input completely compose, at the amplitude level, into a machine with no randomness whatsoever. The probability tables alone could never have predicted this.

nodes.title: A Table That Cannot Come From Rotation
nodes.heading: section
text: Let ω=e^2π i/3 and consider the three-by-three discrete Fourier matrix
[equation]

Every entry of U has magnitude 1/3, so squaring every entry gives a probability table with every one of its nine entries equal to 1/3: uniform, completely featureless at the level of probability. The question is whether some real orthogonal matrix O could also square, entrywise, to this same uniform table. That would require every entry of O to equal plus or minus 1/3, and orthogonality would then require every pair of distinct rows, each written as a sequence of three plus and minus signs, to be exactly balanced against each other. A three-by-three grid of signs with that balancing property is called a Hadamard matrix, and a short, complete check of all five hundred and twelve possible sign patterns across the full nine-entry grid turns up none that qualifies. Three is simply the wrong size for such a grid to exist. So this one uniform table, entirely ordinary as a probability table, has a complex origin and provably no real one.

nodes.heading: section

Every pair among these three bases is mutually unbiased: any vector from one basis overlaps every vector of another with probability exactly one half, the maximal possible mismatch. Try to reproduce this with three real lines in the ordinary plane instead. If Z sits at angle zero and X at forty-five degrees (the real angle giving fifty-fifty overlap with Z), then Y must sit forty-five degrees from Z, which forces Y to sit at either forty-five or negative forty-five degrees. But Y must also sit forty-five degrees from X, which forces Y to sit at either zero or ninety degrees. No single angle satisfies both demands at once. The complex vectors above have an extra freedom, the relative phase carried by i, that lets all three conditions be met simultaneously. Real lines in a flat plane simply run out of room.

nodes.title: The Problem of Two Systems
nodes.heading: chapter
text: So far the same system has been viewed through different contexts or carried through successive transformations. Quantum theory becomes more demanding when two systems are considered together. Composition now means more than doing one thing after another. It means constructing a joint state space whose local parts remain identifiable while new correlations become possible.

Classically, the rule seems obvious. If system A has several distinguishable alternatives and system B has several, the joint alternatives are all ordered pairs. Probability distributions over those pairs include both independent states and correlations. The marginal state of A is obtained by summing over B, and vice versa.

Quantum theory uses a tensor product. A basis for A combined with a basis for B produces a product basis for the composite. Product states describe independent preparations, while superpositions and mixtures generate richer joint states. The tensor product is so deeply built into the standard formalism that it can appear inevitable.

It is not inevitable in the sense required by a foundational reconstruction. The ordinary Kronecker representation of the tensor product is a choice with powerful virtues, but recent real-number reconstructions show that equivalent empirical predictions can be organized using a different composition rule. Complex numbers may disappear from the visible scalar notation while the structural role ordinarily performed by multiplication by i migrates into the way composites are assembled.

This is a textbook case of bottleneck migration. Removing a mathematical object from one location does not necessarily remove the work it performed. The constraint reappears elsewhere. A real formulation of complex quantum theory may replace complex scalars with larger real matrices, an auxiliary two-dimensional structure, a quotient, or a modified tensor operation. The representation changes; the invariant burden remains.

The monograph uses ordinary Kronecker composition through its main comparison of real, complex, and quaternionic theories. Under that convention, the dimensions of their state spaces behave differently. Complex quantum theory possesses exactly the number of joint parameters predicted from local parameter counts. Real quantum theory has extra joint directions invisible to local measurements. A naive quaternionic theory has too few joint degrees of freedom relative to the same product count.

This result is conditional but illuminating. It says that complex quantum mechanics is a fixed point of a particular demand: combine systems in the ordinary way and require the joint state to be completely determined by correlations among local measurements. The fixed point is not metaphysical proof that nature uses complex numbers. It is a precise agreement among scalar field, state-space dimension, and composition rule.

The broader lesson is that a theory of parts is incomplete without a theory of combination. Two formalisms that look different at the level of isolated systems may become equivalent once their composition laws are compared. Conversely, two formalisms that agree locally may diverge only when independent systems are joined. Composition is not housekeeping performed after a theory has been built. It is part of the theory's empirical content.

nodes.title: What the Parts Cannot See
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Local tomography is the principle that a joint state can be determined by statistics obtained from local measurements and their correlations. For ordinary complex quantum systems in finite dimensions, the parameter count works exactly. If we know enough about A, enough about B, and enough about how their local observables correlate, there is no additional joint parameter hiding outside that scheme.

Real quantum theory, under ordinary tensor composition, contains an extra direction. For two two-level real systems, the locally generated symmetric observables span nine dimensions, while the full real symmetric state space has ten. One coefficient remains. It is represented by the product of two antisymmetric generators, conventionally written J times J.

The striking feature of this direction is that it disappears under either partial trace. Inspect system A alone and it is gone. Inspect system B alone and it is gone. It belongs wholly to the relation between them, yet it cannot be reconstructed from the standard inventory of products of locally admissible real observables.

This is not merely an abstract missing number. A family of valid positive states can vary continuously along this direction while keeping both marginals fixed. Except at its central point, the family is entangled when interpreted within real quantum theory. Reinterpret the same matrices within complex quantum theory, and the entire family becomes separable through an explicit decomposition into product states.

Entanglement is therefore not intrinsic to a bare matrix. It is relative to the theory's admissible local states, effects, scalar field, and composition rule. The same array of numbers can mark an inseparable relation in one theory and an ordinary mixture in another.

This should temper claims that a mathematical representation simply displays the ontology. A density matrix acquires physical meaning only within a larger grammar specifying which preparations count as local, which measurements are available, how systems combine, and which decompositions are admissible. Change the grammar and the classification can change while every entry in the matrix remains fixed.

The word grammar is worth taking literally for a moment. Asking whether a matrix is entangled, relative to a fixed theory of composition, is closer to asking whether a sentence is grammatical than to asking whether a rock is heavy. The words on the page do not change depending on which language's rules a reader applies to them, and neither do the numbers in the matrix. But grammaticality is not a property of the words alone; it is a property of the words relative to a set of rules, and the same string of words can be well formed under one grammar and ill formed under another. Entanglement, on this reading, is a fact about fit between a state and a background theory, not a fact about the state read in isolation, and the fit can change even when nothing about the state itself does.

The marginally invisible direction also echoes a recurrent theme in complex systems: some organization exists only at the level of relation and vanishes when either participant is examined alone. But the analogy must be disciplined. Not every emergent or relational property is a quantum correlation. The value of this example is that invisibility is exact. The partial trace annihilates the direction algebraically, and the field-relative separability test identifies precisely what the local theory cannot synthesize.
What the parts cannot see may still be part of the whole. Yet whether it counts as irreducible depends on what operations the parts are allowed to perform.

nodes.title: Why Complex Numbers Keep Returning
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Complex numbers combine two real coordinates with a rule for rotation. Multiplication by i turns one axis into the other and squares to minus one. In elementary geometry, the same action can be represented by a real two-by-two quarter-turn matrix. Nothing about this equivalence is uniquely quantum.

Why, then, do complex numbers recur so persistently in quantum mechanics? Because they package magnitude and orientation into a form whose multiplication naturally composes scaling and rotation. They are an extraordinarily efficient language for the relational memory probabilities discard.

One can translate complex vectors and matrices into larger real ones. The price is an added structural flag that records which real directions form a complex pair. Global complex phase becomes a coordinated real rotation in that auxiliary plane. The symbol i disappears, but its organizational role remains as an operator J satisfying J squared equals negative one.

This distinction between symbol and structure prevents two opposite exaggerations. The first says that complex numbers must be literal ingredients of physical reality because quantum equations contain i. The second says that complex numbers are dispensable and therefore play no fundamental role. The realification shows that the notation is dispensable. It does not show that the rotation-like structure, phase relations, or compatible composition rules are dispensable.

The right question is not "Are complex numbers real?" but "Which invariant work must any empirically adequate representation perform?" A successful real theory must preserve interference, tensorial composition, locality, measurement statistics, and phase redistribution. If it does so by moving complex structure into matrices or quotients, it has changed the location of the mechanism rather than eliminated it.

The monograph calls rotation-scaling maps amplitwists. The name is useful at the popular level because it resists treating complex multiplication as an arbitrary algebraic spell. An amplitwist scales and turns. Composing amplitwists multiplies their scales and adds their turns. Complex multiplication is exactly this action written compactly.

Once viewed this way, complex quantum mechanics becomes less mysterious but not less distinctive. Its amplitudes are not peculiar because they use numbers invented for square roots of negatives. They are powerful because they furnish a closed compositional language for orientations that remain invisible after squaring to probabilities.

It is worth asking why quaternions, the further extension of complex numbers that adds two more independent square roots of minus one, do not simply improve on the same task rather than complex numbers. Under the ordinary way of counting parameters used later in this book, quaternionic composition fails in the opposite direction from real composition. Real composites, as the next part shows, contain joint directions that no product of local descriptions can reach: the local count comes up short. The naive quaternionic product runs the other way, supplying more local-product parameters than the proposed joint state space can independently hold: the local count overshoots. Complex Hermitian state spaces sit exactly at the point where neither failure occurs. This does not prove a quaternionic theory is impossible, since quaternionic composition involves further choices this book does not explore, but it does explain why simply adding more turning directions is not, by itself, an improvement: two extra turning directions do not fit any better than zero extra turning directions do. Only one extra turning direction fits exactly.

nodes.title: The Field Is Not the Theory
nodes.heading: chapter
text: It is tempting to classify physical theories by their number systems: classical physics is real, quantum physics is complex, speculative alternatives may be quaternionic. This shorthand confuses a component with an architecture.

A scalar field tells us how coefficients add and multiply. A physical theory also specifies a state space, transformations, effects, composition, equivalences, dynamics, and an interpretation linking formal objects to laboratory procedures. None of these is fixed by the scalar field alone.

Real, complex, and quaternionic Hilbert spaces support different dimensions of Hermitian operators. Under a shared, naive composition convention, that difference creates a clean local-tomography comparison. But change the representation of composition and a real theory can reproduce complex quantum predictions. The empirical theory is carried by the whole network of constraints, not by the visible alphabet used for coefficients.

This is why representation independence matters. When a derivation concludes that some familiar object is necessary, we should ask whether the result identifies an invariant structure or merely rules out alternatives within one coordinate convention. If a real matrix representation performs exactly the work of complex multiplication, a proof excluding entrywise-real amplitudes has not excluded all real encodings. It has excluded a narrower realization.

The same discipline applies beyond number systems. A particular tensor product, basis, gauge, or state parametrization may be convenient without being forced. A reconstruction becomes stronger when it distinguishes what the data require from how one chosen formalism realizes the requirement.

This does not make every representation equally illuminating. Some expose locality while others hide it. Some make composition transparent while others require cumbersome constraints. Some display symmetries directly. Explanatory economy is a legitimate virtue even when metaphysical uniqueness is unavailable.

Complex Hilbert space may therefore be privileged without being ontologically mandatory. It can be the smallest, clearest, or most natural representation in which the relevant operations close and the local-to-global relations remain visible. That is a substantial claim, though different from saying the universe is made of complex numbers.

nodes.title: Interlude: Two Systems in Coordinates
nodes.heading: chapter
text: As before, the claims of the last three chapters can be checked directly. The calculations below are slightly more involved than the earlier interlude, since two systems are now in play rather than one, but they use nothing beyond ordinary matrix multiplication and can again be skipped without loss by a reader who prefers to take the prose argument on trust.

nodes.title: Nine Directions or Ten
nodes.heading: section
text: A single real two-level system has exactly three independent real symmetric two-by-two matrices available to it as local observables:

Products of these, one drawn from each of two separate systems, give nine independent joint observables, {I,X,Z}{I,X,Z}. But the full space of real symmetric four-by-four matrices, the space that a genuine composite state must live inside, has dimension ten, not nine. The fourth generator needed to complete a full basis of two-by-two real matrices is
[equation]

which is antisymmetric rather than symmetric, so it is not itself an admissible local observable in the real theory: no local measurement on a single real system corresponds to J. Yet the product J J is symmetric, since flipping the sign twice cancels, and it turns out to be linearly independent of all nine products built from {I,X,Z}. This is the missing tenth direction, built from two individually forbidden ingredients whose combination is nonetheless a perfectly legitimate joint observable.

nodes.title: A State That Only Half Can See
nodes.heading: section
text: Consider the one-parameter family of candidate joint states
[equation]

Since J^2=-I, it follows that (J J)^2=I I, so J J has eigenvalues plus and minus one, each occurring twice. The eigenvalues of ρ(c) are therefore 14(1+c) and 14(1-c), each doubly degenerate, and both are nonnegative exactly when c lies between negative one and positive one. Inside that entire range, ρ(c) is a perfectly legitimate physical state.

Now examine what either local observer, restricted to just one of the two systems, actually sees. Since J is traceless, tracing out either system kills the J J term completely, leaving both marginal descriptions equal to the featureless, maximally uncertain state 12 I, for every single value of c in the entire allowed range. An entire interval of genuinely different joint states is completely indistinguishable from either system's own point of view.

nodes.title: The Same Numbers, Two Verdicts
nodes.heading: section
text: Within the real theory, no honest mixture of independent local states can ever produce a nonzero amount of J J: for any real symmetric local state ρ_A, the quantity tr(ρ_A J) is forced to zero by the antisymmetry of J alone, so every product state, and hence every mixture of product states, contributes nothing along that direction. Since tr[ρ(c)(J J)]=c, any nonzero c is therefore entangled, by direct calculation, within real quantum theory.

Within the complex theory, the very same matrix tells a different story. Since J equals -i times the ordinary complex Pauli matrix σ_y, the product J J equals -σ_yσ_y, and ρ(c) can be rewritten explicitly, entry for entry, as
