a mixture of four ordinary complex product states with nonnegative weights summing to one, for every c in the allowed range. The identical array of sixteen numbers is entangled under one theory's rules for admissible local states and separable under the other's. Nothing about the matrix changed between the two paragraphs above. Only the background theory of what a legitimate local state is allowed to be did.

nodes.title: A State Is Not Yet a Context
nodes.heading: chapter
text: The early reconstruction concerns transitions between complete measurement contexts: entire orthonormal frames compared with one another. Standard quantum mechanics also speaks of an individual prepared state. Passing from a frame to a state requires a bridge.

Mathematically, any normalized vector can be completed into an orthonormal basis. Operationally, however, identifying a preparation with one distinguished member of such a frame is an additional commitment. The technical monograph names it rather than allowing a routine linear-algebra fact to conceal the physical identification.

Once the identification is accepted, the pure-state Born rule appears immediately. The probability of a measurement outcome is one entry in the transition matrix between the preparation frame and the measurement frame. That entry is the squared magnitude of their overlap.

This is best called a recovery rather than an origin story. The squared-amplitude rule is already present in the definition of a unistochastic transition. Treating a state as a selected column transfers that rule from context-to-context comparisons to state-to-outcome probabilities. The achievement is architectural clarity: it shows exactly which bridge turns one use of squared amplitudes into the familiar Born formula.

Classical mixtures then yield density operators. If a preparation procedure chooses among pure states with ordinary probabilities, outcome probabilities must average accordingly. Linearity packages the mixture into a positive, unit-trace operator, and the Born rule becomes a trace formula. Again, the step is not magic. It is the consequence of demanding affine consistency under classical uncertainty.

This layered derivation helps prevent several conflations. A probability vector is not a state vector. A state vector is not an entire context. A pure-state Born rule is not yet the most general measurement rule. A density operator represents both classical mixing and quantum state structure, but different decompositions of the same density operator need not correspond to experimentally distinguishable ensembles.

Popular accounts often collapse these levels into the phrase "the wavefunction gives probabilities." The reconstruction slows the sentence down. A context supplies a family of alternatives; a prepared pure state is represented as a designated vector completable into such a context; overlaps with a measurement context yield probabilities; mixtures extend the rule affinely; generalized measurements require a further dilation argument. Each transition has a cost.

The reward for paying attention is not pedantry. It is the ability to ask where an interpretation enters. Is the state an individual physical condition, an equivalence class of preparations, a catalogue of expectations, or a relation between system and context? The mathematics does not answer automatically. It tells us what operational role the state must play once the bridges are chosen.

nodes.title: Measurements Become Operators
nodes.heading: chapter
text: A laboratory measurement produces outcomes: detector clicks, pointer positions, spectral lines, recorded numbers. Quantum textbooks represent observables by Hermitian operators. Why should those two descriptions be equivalent?

Begin with a sharp measurement, a collection of mutually exclusive projectors that together exhaust the possibilities. Attach a real number to each outcome. The operator formed by multiplying each projector by its label and adding the results is Hermitian. Conversely, the spectral theorem says that every finite-dimensional Hermitian operator can be decomposed into real eigenvalues and orthogonal projectors. The operator and the real-labelled sharp measurement contain the same data.

The point is modest but clarifying. Hermiticity need not be announced as an independent metaphysical property possessed by observables. It follows from packaging mutually exclusive sharp outcomes carrying real labels. The hidden cost is the decision that recorded outcomes are real-valued. That is natural for quantities we compare and average, but it remains a modelling choice.

The familiar eigenvalue rule follows as well. If a state lies entirely within one eigenspace, the corresponding projector returns probability one. "Measuring an observable in an eigenstate yields its eigenvalue with certainty" is not another disconnected axiom once the Born rule and spectral representation are in place.

Generalized measurements require a larger step. A positive-operator-valued measure, or POVM, need not consist of mutually orthogonal projectors on the system's own space. Yet every finite POVM can be represented as a sharp projective measurement on a larger space containing an ancilla. This is Naimark dilation.

Dilation exhibits a recurring architecture: enlarge the description until the operation becomes simple, perform the simple operation there, and then project or trace away the auxiliary structure. Mixed states arise by ignoring part of a larger pure system; generalized measurements arise by performing sharp measurements on a larger composite. What looks nonclassical or unsharp downstairs may be ordinary and sharp upstairs relative to a richer space.

But mathematical dilation does not prove that every laboratory apparatus literally implements a unique hidden sharp measurement. Dilations are generally nonunique. They show representability, not ontology. Once again the witness-mechanism distinction applies: the POVM statistics witness that some dilation exists; they do not identify which physical enlargement, if any, should be regarded as the mechanism.

The practical motivation for POVMs is worth making concrete, because it is easy to read this chapter as pure formalism. Real detectors are imperfect: a photon counter may fail to click even when a photon arrives, a Stern-Gerlach apparatus may be misaligned by some small angle, and an interferometer may leak a little light down the wrong arm. None of these situations is naturally described by a family of perfectly orthogonal projectors, because the apparatus genuinely cannot distinguish every pair of alternatives a sharp measurement would require. Representing such an apparatus by a POVM is not a mathematical convenience layered on top of the true, sharp description. It is often the only honest description available, and the dilation theorem is the guarantee that this honesty need not come at the cost of consistency: whatever the imperfect apparatus is doing, some larger, perfectly sharp measurement scheme would do the same thing, if only the relevant ancilla could be identified and included.

nodes.title: Time Enters Late
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Many presentations begin quantum mechanics with Schrodinger's equation. In this reconstruction, time arrives near the end. This reversal is revealing because it separates the kinematics of admissible states and measurements from the dynamics that carry states through time.

Assume that a closed system evolves reversibly, continuously, and consistently with temporal composition. Evolving for a duration s and then t must equal evolving for s plus t. The evolution operators form a continuous one-parameter unitary group.

In finite dimensions, such a group has a Hermitian generator. Write the group as an exponential and its infinitesimal law is Schrodinger's equation. The equation is therefore the local differential form of continuous reversible composition.

This derivation is mathematically standard, but its placement changes its meaning. Schrodinger's equation is not conjured as a separate law added to an otherwise complete probability calculus. It expresses how the coherent lift varies when the composition parameter is time.

What the argument does not establish is equally important. The Hermitian generator is not automatically identified with physical energy. The constant placed beside it is not automatically Planck's constant. Those identifications require further physical bridges involving time translations, units, experiment, and the classical limit. Nor does the unitary group describe open systems, measurements, dissipation, or irreversible thermodynamic processes without enlargement or approximation.

Continuity itself is assumed. Discrete time, stochastic dynamics, nonlinear evolution, and nonunitary fundamental laws are not eliminated merely because a continuous unitary assumption yields the standard equation elegantly. A reconstruction shows what follows from its premises; elegance does not retroactively derive the premises.

Still, the result reinforces the book's central motif. Exact compositional closure lives upstairs. At the projected level, probabilities may appear to mix, spread, or lose information. At the amplitude level, closed evolution is reversible and group-like. Irreversibility enters through restriction, coarse-graining, environmental coupling, or an explicitly different dynamics.

nodes.title: Inside the Birkhoff Polytope
nodes.heading: chapter
text: For a fixed number of alternatives, every bistochastic matrix lives inside a geometric body called the Birkhoff polytope. Its corners are permutation matrices: perfectly definite relabellings. Every other point is a weighted average of these corners. The polytope is therefore the complete landscape of classical mixing transformations that preserve the uniform distribution.

Unistochastic matrices occupy a region inside this landscape. Each comes from a unitary matrix after all complex phases have been erased by taking squared magnitudes. Orthostochastic matrices form a still more restrictive region obtained from real orthogonal matrices.
The direction of inclusion matters: orthostochastic matrices sit inside unistochastic matrices, which sit inside bistochastic matrices.

Quantum admissibility does not fill gaps that classical bistochasticity cannot reach. The opposite is true at the level of individual transition matrices: classical normalization and mixing permit probability tables that cannot arise as transitions between orthonormal quantum contexts of the same dimension. Quantum coherence imposes additional geometric constraints.

For two alternatives all three regions coincide. The Birkhoff polytope is merely a line segment, and every point on it has both a real and complex coherent lift. This is why two-by-two probability data cannot by itself reveal whether real or complex amplitudes lie behind it.

At three alternatives the geometry becomes genuinely interesting. The bistochastic set has four dimensions. The unistochastic region is full-dimensional but does not occupy the whole polytope, and its boundary is curved rather than simply formed by flat faces. Orthostochastic matrices lie along a special subset of that boundary. The uniform matrix sits at the center and is unistochastic, realized by the three-dimensional Fourier matrix, yet it is not orthostochastic.

This means there are two distinct geometrical questions. The first asks whether a point in the classical polytope has any unitary lift. The second asks how many inequivalent lifts it has and how those lifts fit together across paths and cycles. Membership and reconstruction are not the same problem.

For three dimensions, unistochasticity can be tested through a triangle condition. After suitable normalization, orthogonality between two rows of a prospective unitary requires three complex contributions to close into a triangle. Their lengths are determined by products of matrix entries. If the largest length exceeds the sum of the other two, no choice of phases can close the figure and the bistochastic matrix is not unistochastic. At the boundary the triangle flattens. Inside, two mirror-image phase choices commonly remain.

This is a rare gift to intuition: a hidden-phase existence problem becomes ordinary Euclidean closure. The probability entries determine lengths but not directions. Unitary admissibility asks whether directions can be assigned so the weighted contributions cancel exactly.

For four or more alternatives no comparably simple complete picture is known. The unistochastic region is non-convex, its fibres can change dimension, and phase constraints couple many orthogonality equations. Averaging two unistochastic matrices need not produce another unistochastic matrix even though both and their average remain bistochastic. Coherent realizability is not stable under classical mixture at the level of transition matrices.

The Birkhoff polytope should thus be understood as a possibility space, and the unistochastic region as an admissibility geography drawn inside it. Boundaries mark probability transitions at which a coherent lift appears, disappears, or becomes degenerate. Studying those boundaries can constrain possible experiments without requiring us to expand every state vector explicitly. Geometry performs part of the bookkeeping normally assigned to amplitudes.

nodes.title: The Cliff at Three Dimensions
nodes.heading: chapter
text: The triangle of earlier chapters took real work to build. Three contexts, not two; a closed loop, not a single comparison; a careful argument about what a cycle can carry that no edge along it can carry alone. It is worth asking why the obstruction needed all of that machinery. The answer turns out to be a low-dimensional accident, and once it is named, an entire dimension's worth of extra structure collapses away.

Recall the degenerate coincidence from early on: at two outcomes, every real orthogonal lift is automatically a legitimate unitary lift as well, and vice versa. A single transition table, at that size, simply cannot tell the two number systems apart. This is precisely why the triangle was needed. If no single edge can ever distinguish real from complex admissibility at two outcomes, the only place a difference could possibly show up is in how several edges fit together around a loop, and the earlier chapters went looking for exactly that.

At three outcomes, this coincidence has already been shown to fail. The uniform three-by-three table, the one built from squaring the entries of the Fourier matrix, has a complex origin and provably no real one. That fact was established with nothing more than a single transition table and a short argument about the nonexistence of a certain sign pattern. No loop was involved. No second or third context was needed. One table, on its own, already refuses a real lift.

Put these two facts side by side and something striking follows. At two outcomes, the cheapest possible demonstration that real and complex admissibility differ requires an entire closed loop of three contexts, because no single edge can show the difference at that size. At three outcomes and above, the cheapest possible demonstration is a single edge, because individual tables can already show the difference on their own. What collapses is not the witness itself but the graph-theoretic complexity needed to state one: from a closed loop with cycle rank one down to a graph with cycle rank zero, a single edge carrying one nontrivial label. The edge itself, the actual unistochastic table with no orthostochastic lift, still has to be exhibited; nothing about it comes for free. What disappears is the need to close a loop at all.

This is worth restating plainly because it runs against the natural expectation that more outcomes should demand more elaborate machinery to say anything interesting. Here the opposite happens. The triangle earned its keep specifically because two-outcome tables are unusually uninformative about the underlying number system, an accident of that particular size rather than a general feature of how real and complex admissibility relate. Once that accident is no longer in force, the elaborate cycle-closing argument is no longer needed to settle the question the triangle was built to settle. A birthday-party magic trick that takes an elaborate setup to pull off at one table size turns out to have a one-line version at every larger table size, once the specific reason the setup was needed in the first place goes away.

None of this makes the triangle's argument obsolete, and it does not make cycles uninteresting once outcomes number three or more. The triangle answers a narrower and, in its own way, harder question than mere existence of a difference: can data that individually passes every single test still fail once several tests are required to agree with one another simultaneously. That question is not touched by a single misbehaving table, however dramatic, because a single table is exactly what the cycle question sets aside from the start. Whether cycles built from individually well-behaved edges can still fail to glue once outcomes number three or more remains, at the time of writing, an open question, and answering it would require the triangle's style of argument rather than the single-table argument of this chapter. What has been settled is a cheaper, blunter question: does a difference between the two number systems exist at all, at this size. From three outcomes onward, one badly behaved table is already enough to answer yes.

nodes.title: Drawing the Forbidden Region
nodes.heading: chapter
text: How might one map the unistochastic region in practice? The naive method samples unitary matrices, projects them to squared magnitudes, and plots the resulting points. This produces useful pictures in low-dimensional slices, but it cannot prove that an apparently empty region is truly forbidden. Rare or thin sets may simply be missed.

A complementary method begins with bistochastic matrices and attempts phase retrieval. The magnitudes of the unitary entries are fixed as square roots of the given probabilities. Unknown phases are then adjusted to satisfy row and column orthogonality. The residual failure of those equations supplies a numerical distance from realizability, though global optimization is required because local minima can imitate obstructions.

Semialgebraic methods offer a more exact route. Replace each complex phase with real and imaginary components constrained to the unit circle, write orthogonality as polynomial equations, and eliminate the hidden variables. The resulting inequalities describe the projection of the unitary group into probability space. In principle, quantifier elimination can characterize the boundary. In practice, its cost rises rapidly with dimension.

Optimization provides another view. Given a bistochastic matrix, minimize the distance between it and the squared magnitudes of a candidate unitary. A zero minimum certifies unistochasticity up to numerical tolerance; a positive global lower bound certifies exclusion. Riemannian optimization on the unitary group respects the constraint surface more naturally than unconstrained adjustment of matrix entries.

One can also search the boundary by monitoring the Jacobian of the projection from unitary parameters to bistochastic coordinates. Critical values indicate folds, cusps, and changes in the number of lifts. Rather than asking only whether a matrix is admissible, this approach studies how stable its admissibility is under perturbation.

The most informative computational atlas would combine these methods. Sampling would reveal broad shape; phase optimization would classify candidate points; exact inequalities would certify selected slices; Jacobian analysis would locate singular boundaries; and continuation methods would follow boundary components as external parameters change.

Such an atlas would not merely decorate the theory. It would distinguish robustly admissible transitions from those balanced precariously at the edge of coherent realizability. It could identify extremal matrices that separate real, complex, and quaternionic lifts, locate minimal witnesses for competing composition rules, and suggest experiments concentrated near regions where the theories disagree most strongly.

The algorithmic challenge is itself an instance of what probability forgets. We are given the magnitudes and asked whether compatible orientations exist. The search space consists almost entirely of information deliberately removed by projection.

nodes.title: The Phase-Retrieval Problem
nodes.heading: chapter
text: If a unitary matrix is projected to a unistochastic matrix, what can be recovered? At minimum, multiplying rows or columns by phases changes the unitary but not its squared magnitudes. These transformations are gauge freedoms relative to the transition probabilities. Complex conjugation also preserves all magnitudes. Beyond these obvious ambiguities, some probability matrices admit several inequivalent lifts, while exceptional points admit continuous families.

Phase retrieval asks whether magnitudes determine a compatible object and, if so, how uniquely. Versions of the problem appear in crystallography, optics, signal processing, and astronomy. A detector often records intensity, proportional to the squared magnitude of a wave, while discarding its phase. Reconstructing the source then requires constraints, redundancy, multiple illuminations, or prior information.

In quantum transitions, one probability matrix usually cannot reconstruct the full unitary. Additional contexts can help, but they introduce gluing constraints. Sequential experiments can reveal relative phases indirectly through interference. What was invisible in one projection becomes visible when the unknown transformation is composed with a known reference transformation.

This gives a practical meaning to phase. Phase is not directly read from a single intensity record, but neither is it forever metaphysically inaccessible. It is relationally observable: change the experimental context so that phase affects a later magnitude. The hidden variable becomes manifest through controlled continuation.

Some information, however, remains gauge. A global phase applied to a state changes no quantum prediction. More generally, phase conventions attached independently to basis vectors alter the matrix representation without altering the physical transition probabilities. The retrieval problem must therefore recover an equivalence class, not an absolute list of phases.

This distinction is essential. Projection removes both genuine physical relations and arbitrary representational choices. A good reconstruction should recover the former without pretending to recover the latter. Gauge quotienting is not information loss in the same sense as erasing a relative phase that later affects interference. One removes redundant descriptions; the other merges operationally distinguishable continuations.

The geometry of fibres, the collection of all unitaries projecting to the same probability matrix, organizes these possibilities. A small discrete fibre means the probabilities nearly determine the coherent lift after gauge is removed. A large fibre means substantial underdetermination. Singular fibres often occur at symmetric or boundary points and may signal enhanced freedom or instability.

Thus the unistochastic matrix can serve as a primary object without becoming a complete one. Its geometry tells us which lifts are possible, how many remain, and where additional experiments are required. Treating the matrix as primary means beginning inquiry from observable constraints, not declaring that the observable shadow contains its own mechanism.

nodes.title: Decoherence and the Routes Downward
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Closed quantum evolution is unitary, but laboratory systems are rarely closed. They interact with environments containing enormous numbers of degrees of freedom. The joint system may evolve coherently while the subsystem we observe follows an apparently irreversible, noisy trajectory.

The basic operation is familiar from earlier chapters: enlarge, evolve, then forget. Prepare a system together with an environment, apply a joint unitary transformation, and trace over the environmental degrees of freedom. The resulting map on the system is a quantum channel. It need not be unitary or reversible.

If we monitor only populations in a preferred basis, some channels induce ordinary stochastic evolution. Under special conditions the resulting population-transition matrix may be unistochastic: its entries are squared magnitudes of an effective unitary. But general open-system dynamics is broader. Coupling to an environment can produce channels whose population maps are merely stochastic, and the full channel acts on coherences as well as populations.

Decoherence is the progressive loss of accessible phase relations into environmental correlations. It does not necessarily destroy information at the level of the global closed system. It redistributes information so widely that local interference becomes impractical or impossible to recover. The environment acquires records of alternatives, and those records suppress the cross terms visible to local measurements.

This supplies a physical route from coherent amplitudes to classical-looking probabilities. Yet the route is not a simple replacement of quantum dynamics by a stochastic matrix. Different channels can induce the same population dynamics while treating coherence differently. A classical transition table may therefore conceal not only phases of a unitary but the entire manner in which coherence leaked into an environment.

Entropy illustrates the distinction. A bistochastic map on a classical probability distribution cannot decrease Shannon entropy. A unital quantum channel likewise cannot decrease von Neumann entropy in the same unrestricted way, though the precise statements depend on dimension and assumptions. Non-unital channels, such as cooling or amplitude damping, can decrease the system's entropy by transferring it elsewhere. Entropy production is a property of the system-environment accounting, not merely of a local stochastic shadow.

Connecting quantum uncertainty directly to classical mixing therefore requires care. Majorization gives exact ordering results for bistochastic maps. Decoherence can often be represented as movement toward more mixed reduced states. But thermodynamic entropy production also depends on energy, reservoirs, correlations, and what is counted as the system. A flattened probability distribution is evidence of mixing, not a complete thermodynamic balance sheet.

The projection framework clarifies what must be tracked. At each downward step, unitary to channel, channel to populations, populations to coarse-grained records, new distinctions are discarded. Each projection has its own fibres, its own compositional failures, and its own conditions under which lost information can return. Decoherence is not one act of forgetting but a pathway through several layers of admissibility.

nodes.title: The Foundational Cost Ledger
nodes.heading: chapter
text: A reconstruction earns trust not by having no assumptions, but by showing where each assumption enters and what it purchases. The technical monograph lists four explicit operational additions: local tomography; the representation of pure states as designated vectors completable into frames; real-valued measurement labels; and continuous reversible time evolution.

Those four are real costs, but they are not the total cost of the reconstruction. They are the assumptions added after a framework has already been selected. The framework includes finite-dimensional probability spaces, bistochastic transitions, unistochastic admissibility, frame-based contexts, convex mixtures, finite-dimensional Hilbert-space machinery, and a chosen rule for composing systems.

The distinction can be made cleanly by keeping a two-level ledger. Framework commitments define the arena and the meaning of admissibility. Operational bridge assumptions connect objects in that arena to preparations, measurements, composites, and time. Mathematical theorems then derive consequences conditional on both levels.

This resolves a misleading tension. It is true that the Born rule, Hermitian-observable correspondence, eigenvalue rule, Schrodinger equation, and finite POVM dilation need not be postulated independently once the chosen architecture is in place. It is also true that the architecture contains quantum-shaped commitments, especially unistochastic admissibility. Both statements can stand without contradiction.

The phrase "four assumptions" should therefore be read locally: four additional operational assumptions beyond the prior admissibility framework. Used as a total foundational count, it understates the premises. Used as a dependency claim, it is informative. It shows that several textbook postulates are interconnected consequences rather than isolated declarations.

This style of auditing is itself a contribution. Reconstructions often slide between derivation, representation, equivalence, and empirical identification. A formula may be derived from definitions but still depend on a physical bridge connecting those definitions to the world. A structure may reproduce quantum predictions without being uniquely required. A familiar postulate may become a theorem only because an equally strong condition was placed upstream.

None of these observations invalidates the reconstruction. They specify what kind of achievement it is. The book does not manufacture quantum mechanics from featureless chance. It begins from a constrained family of probabilistic shadows and reconstructs the coherent architecture capable of casting them and composing them.

An ordinary, non-quantum example makes the two-tier ledger easier to hold onto. A building inspector who signs off on a house is not certifying that the house was built from nothing. The framework, foundation codes, wiring standards, material specifications, was already fixed by the jurisdiction long before the inspection began, and nobody lists the entire building code as a cost of any particular house. What the inspector's signature adds, on top of that fixed framework, are the specific, checkable facts about this house: the beam spans meet the load requirements, the outlets are grounded, the smoke detectors are present and wired correctly. Asked what the inspection cost, in the sense of what it specifically certified, the honest answer names those few checked items, not the whole code they were checked against. Asked what the house cost, in the sense of everything that had to be true for it to be a legal house at all, the honest answer includes the code as well. Both questions are legitimate. They are simply different questions, and the reconstruction's four assumptions answer the first one, not the second.

nodes.title: Witnesses, Mechanisms, and Admissibility
nodes.heading: chapter
text: The monograph's implications extend beyond quantum foundations because its logical distinctions are portable. A witness is an observable pattern compatible with a process. A mechanism is a structure that generates the pattern and supports interventions and continuations. An admissibility condition specifies which candidate mechanisms are allowed.

One witness may have many mechanisms. One mechanism may cast many witnesses in different contexts. A collection of individually valid witnesses may admit no single common mechanism. These three facts organize much of scientific inference.

Moments of a distribution witness its shape without identifying the causal process that generated it. Neural activity may witness a perceptual distinction without establishing consciousness, unity, or subjecthood. A linguistic output may witness competent task performance without identifying the internal algorithm. A historical inscription may witness an event while omitting the social relations required to interpret it. In every case, projection preserves some claims and blocks others.

The quantum example adds a sharper point: omitted structure can be operationally dormant at one stage and decisive at the next. We cannot judge sufficiency once and for all. A representation adequate for classification may fail for composition; one adequate for local prediction may fail for global gluing; one adequate for marginals may fail for entanglement; one adequate for populations may fail for decoherence.

Admissibility is therefore task-relative without being arbitrary. The task specifies which operations must be preserved. If we need only reproduce a single probability table, many lifts may suffice. If we need sequential composition, relative phase matters. If we need a global family of contexts, cycle consistency matters. If we need composite systems, tensor structure and local tomography matter.

This suggests a general research discipline: before claiming that a compressed statistic captures a phenomenon, state the operations under which it must remain sufficient. Then test whether the projection preserves those operations. Failures should not be dismissed as anomalies. They identify the missing structure.

Across every worked case in this book, real or composite, single system or joint, the failure takes the same shape, and it is worth stating that shape once, plainly, now that all the pieces are in view. Something looks entirely fine examined locally: an edge, a marginal, a single probability table. Something breaks only when that local description is asked to compose, glue, or generalize: two transformations chained together, three contexts closed into a loop, two systems joined into one. The break is repaired by structure that was not visible in the local data and could not have been read off it. That repairing structure can typically be written down in more than one way, real or complex, one composition convention or another, and the different notations are not equally revealing even when they are equally correct. What ultimately matters is the invariant work the structure performs, the compositions it closes and the distinctions it preserves, not which alphabet happens to carry that work in a given presentation.

Probability, in this sense, tells you the weights. It does not tell you the orientations. And orientations, again and again in this book, are exactly what determine how one thing connects to the next.
Quantum mechanics becomes, on this reading, the most exact demonstration that continuation can reveal what observation forgot.

nodes.title: What This Does Not Solve
nodes.heading: chapter
text: No reconstruction of formal structure automatically resolves the measurement problem. Showing why amplitudes are needed for compositional closure does not specify why one outcome is experienced, whether collapse is physical, or how probabilities should be interpreted. It constrains the arena in which those questions are asked.

Nor does the reconstruction derive the complex field uniquely. Real and quaternionic alternatives can be compared under specified assumptions, and complex quantum theory enjoys striking compositional virtues. But empirically equivalent real formulations can relocate complex structure into representation and composition. The invariant requirement is stronger than bare real probability and weaker than literal complex-number ontology. On the quaternionic side, a structural bound now exists showing that quaternionic mutually unbiased bases could in principle outnumber complex ones by roughly a factor of two, but this is only an upper bound: nobody has yet exhibited a quaternionic configuration that actually exceeds the complex count, and even if one were found, translating it into a genuine separation witness of the kind this book builds elsewhere would take further work not yet done.

The approach also remains finite-dimensional. Infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces introduce domains of unbounded operators, topological subtleties, continuous spectra, and a genuinely nontrivial version of Stone's theorem. Quantum field theory adds locality, relativistic covariance, particle creation, inequivalent representations, and renormalization. Nothing in the finite matrix reconstruction should be silently promoted to a solution of those problems.

The Birkhoff-polytope programme is incomplete in higher dimensions. Characterizing all unistochastic matrices, their boundaries, fibres, and extremal points remains difficult. The absence of a simple criterion is not a technical inconvenience peripheral to the thesis; it marks how complicated the relation between observable probabilities and coherent lifts becomes as alternatives multiply.

Open systems require quantum channels rather than transition matrices alone. General measurements require instruments if post-measurement states matter, not merely POVM effects. Thermodynamic claims require an explicit accounting of energy and environment. The probability-shadow perspective organizes these extensions but does not replace them.

Finally, structural explanation is not ontology. The fact that a coherent lift repairs composition does not decide whether the lift is a physical object, an informational device, a relation, or an equivalence class of experimental procedures. The framework tells us what any successful interpretation must preserve. It does not tell us which metaphysical vocabulary should win.
These limits are productive. A theory becomes more credible when it knows the boundary of its own inheritance. Each unsolved problem identifies a bridge not yet earned.

nodes.title: A Research Programme in the Shadow
nodes.heading: chapter
text: The immediate mathematical programme is to map admissibility more fully. In dimensions above three, this means combining exact algebra, numerical optimization, and topology to characterize the unistochastic region inside the Birkhoff polytope. Particular attention should go to boundary singularities, changes in fibre cardinality, and matrices separating scalar fields or composition rules. The cheapest possible witness separating real from complex admissibility is now known at every dimension, a single edge suffices from three outcomes upward, a full cycle only at two, but this leaves the harder cycle-gluing question at three outcomes and above entirely open: can individually well-behaved edges still fail to fit together globally once tables can no longer be told apart one at a time. Settling that question, not the easier existence question this book already closes, is where the real work above two dimensions remains.

A second programme concerns graph-labelled transitions. Rather than studying a single matrix, one studies networks of contexts whose edges carry probability data. The central questions become minimal obstruction, forbidden subgraphs, robustness under noise, and the complexity of deciding global realizability. Approximate gluing is especially important experimentally: exact algebraic inconsistency must be replaced by quantitative distance from the nearest realizable model.

A third programme tracks successive projections in open systems. Starting from a system-environment unitary, one can compare the information lost in forming a channel, in restricting to population dynamics, and in coarse-graining recorded outcomes. Different projections may destroy different composition laws. Their hierarchy could connect phase retrieval, decoherence, and entropy production without treating them as one undifferentiated loss.

A fourth programme compares representations. If complex quantum theory can be recoded over real numbers using a modified tensor product or quotient, which properties remain manifest and which become nonlocal or cumbersome? Can the triangle and local-tomography obstructions be stated in representation-independent terms? Which categorical or operational invariants capture the surviving role of complex structure?

A fifth programme is methodological. The witness-mechanism distinction can be applied wherever scientific practice compresses rich processes into statistics. One can ask of moments, embeddings, biomarkers, institutional metrics, and machine-learning benchmarks what was asked of transition probabilities: Which operations does the summary preserve? What distinctions lie in its fibre? Which cycles or compositions make those distinctions observable again?
These projects share a single movement. Begin from the shadow, characterize the objects capable of casting it, and then test whether those objects remain compatible when the experiment continues.

nodes.title: The World After the Probability
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Probability is among the most successful languages ever devised for reasoning under uncertainty. Nothing in this book diminishes it. The lesson is more exact: probability is a language of weights, and weights alone do not always contain the relations needed for composition.

Quantum theory teaches this through interference. Two processes with the same visible probabilities can differ in how they combine. It teaches it again through context graphs. Pairwise admissible transitions can fail to belong to one global arrangement. It teaches it through composite systems. The same matrix can be entangled or separable depending on the local operations and scalar field that give it meaning. It teaches it through decoherence. Classical-looking trajectories can emerge when phase information flows into an environment beyond local reach.

At each stage a record is truthful within its scope. The failure occurs when truth at one grain is inherited by another without a bridge. A single transition does not determine a sequence. Local consistency does not determine global consistency. Marginals do not determine every joint structure in every theory. Representation does not determine ontology.

The value of a coherent lift is that it restores the operations the shadow cannot perform. But the lift is not free. We choose an admissibility class, a scalar organization, a composition law, and operational bridges. The honest reconstruction states those choices before celebrating what follows from them.

Seen this way, quantum mechanics is neither a revolt against reason nor merely classical ignorance with unusual bookkeeping. It is a theory built around a precise refusal: do not identify the observable distribution with the complete compositional state.
What probability forgets is not noise around the edges of reality. Sometimes it is the orientation by which one possible event meets the next.

nodes.title: A Guide to the Technical Monograph
nodes.heading: chapter
text: The companion's first two parts correspond chiefly to Chapters 1 through 7 of Quantum Mechanics from Admissible Probabilistic Composition. The Cliff at Three Dimensions, in Part V, draws on Chapter 20; the forest-theorem capstone at the end of Trees, Cycles, and the Cost of Agreement draws on Chapter 22. The discussion of composite systems follows Chapters 8 through 12 and 19; the note on real reformulations follows section 18.4; the aside on quaternions in What This Does Not Solve draws on Chapters 21 and 24. The recovery of states, observables, dynamics, and generalized measurements follows Chapters 14 through 17. Readers interested in exact notation, proofs, and the assumption ledgers should use the technical text as the authoritative source.

nodes.title: Further Reading
nodes.heading: chapter
text: For standard quantum mechanics, see J. J. Sakurai and Jim Napolitano, Modern Quantum Mechanics. For the geometry of stochastic and unistochastic matrices, see work by Karol Zyczkowski, Marek Kus, Wojciech Slomczynski, and Hans-Jurgen Sommers. For stochastic-quantum correspondences, see Jacob Barandes. For operational reconstructions and local tomography, see work by Lucien Hardy and the earlier parameter-counting arguments associated with Huzihiro Araki and William Wootters. For real simulations and reformulations of complex quantum theory, consult the recent constructions discussed in section 18.4 of the technical monograph. For a geometric introduction to complex multiplication as rotation and scaling, see Tristan Needham, Visual Complex Analysis.
End of companion manuscript.
